claim: The expansion of huge superfamilies of enzymes, transcriptional regulators, transporters, and signaling molecules from single ancestral genes has been a dominant process in the evolution of life.
source: The expansion of huge superfamilies of enzymes, transcriptional regulators, transporters, and signaling molecules from single ancestral genes has been a dominant process in the evolution of life (Bergthorsson et al., 2007; Chothia et al., 2003; Glasner et al., 2006; Hughes, 1994; Ohno, 1970; Todd et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing this as a well-documented evolutionary process.

claim: The emergence of new protein family members has enabled organisms to access new nutrients, sense new stimuli, and respond to changing conditions with ever more sophistication.
source: The emergence of new protein family members has enabled organisms to access new nutrients, sense new stimuli, and respond to changing conditions with ever more sophistication (Conant and Wolfe, 2008; Nei and Rooney, 2005; Reams and Neidle, 2004; Santos et al., 2017; Starr et al., 2017; Storz, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on the functional consequences of protein family expansion.

claim: The Innovation-Amplification-Divergence (IAD) model posits that evolution of new enzymes by gene duplication and divergence begins when a physiologically irrelevant promiscuous activity becomes important for fitness due to a mutation or environmental change.
source: The Innovation-Amplification-Divergence (IAD) model (Figure 1) posits that evolution of new enzymes by gene duplication and divergence begins when a physiologically irrelevant promiscuous activity becomes important for fitness due to a mutation or environmental change (Bergthorsson et al., 2007; Francino, 2005; Hughes, 1994; Näsvall et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Gene duplication/amplification provides a ready mechanism to improve fitness by increasing the abundance of a weak-link enzyme.
source: Gene duplication/amplification provides a ready mechanism to improve fitness by increasing the abundance of a weak-link enzyme.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the IAD model and is supported by the context of the cited literature.

claim: If mutations lead to an enzyme capable of efficiently carrying out the newly needed function, selective pressure to maintain a high copy number will be removed, allowing extra copies to be lost and leaving behind two paralogs.
source: If mutations lead to an enzyme capable of efficiently carrying out the newly needed function, selective pressure to maintain a high copy number will be removed, allowing extra copies to be lost and leaving behind two paralogs (or just one gene encoding a new enzyme if the original function is no longer needed).
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical understanding of the IAD model and evolutionary principles.

claim: Näsvall et al. used laboratory evolution to demonstrate that a gene encoding an enzyme with two inefficient activities required for synthesis of histidine and tryptophan amplified and diverged to alleles encoding two specialists within 2000 generations.
source: In a landmark study, Näsvall et al. used laboratory evolution to demonstrate that a gene encoding an enzyme with two inefficient activities required for synthesis of histidine and tryptophan amplified and diverged to alleles encoding two specialists within 2000 generations (Näsvall et al., 2012; Newton et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The Näsvall et al. study followed only mutations in the diverging gene.
source: However, this study followed only mutations in the diverging gene.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' interpretation of the cited study.

claim: When an organism is exposed to a novel selection pressure that requires evolution of a new enzyme, any mutation – either in the gene encoding the weak-link enzyme or elsewhere in the genome – that improves fitness will provide a selective advantage.
source: When an organism is exposed to a novel selection pressure that requires evolution of a new enzyme, any mutation – either in the gene encoding the weak-link enzyme or elsewhere in the genome – that improves fitness will provide a selective advantage.
evidence: This claim is based on established evolutionary principles.

claim: ProA (γ-glutamyl phosphate reductase) is essential for proline synthesis in E. coli.
source: ProA (γ-glutamyl phosphate reductase, Figure 2) is essential for proline synthesis in E. coli.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2 and is established knowledge about E. coli metabolism.

claim: ArgC (N-acetylglutamyl phosphate reductase) catalyzes a similar reaction in the arginine synthesis pathway.
source: ArgC (N-acetylglutamyl phosphate reductase) catalyzes a similar reaction in the arginine synthesis pathway, although the two enzymes are not homologous (Goto et al., 2003; Ludovice et al., 1992; Page et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ProA and ArgC are not homologous.
source: ArgC (N-acetylglutamyl phosphate reductase) catalyzes a similar reaction in the arginine synthesis pathway, although the two enzymes are not homologous (Goto et al., 2003; Ludovice et al., 1992; Page et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ProA can reduce N-acetylglutamyl phosphate (NAGP), but its activity is too inefficient to support growth of a ∆argC strain of E. coli in glucose.
source: ProA can reduce N-acetylglutamyl phosphate (NAGP), but its activity is too inefficient to support growth of a ∆argC strain of E. coli in glucose.
evidence: This claim is based on prior experimental work by the authors' group.

claim: A point mutation that changes Glu383 to Ala in ProA allows slow growth of the ∆argC strain in glucose.
source: However, a point mutation that changes Glu383 to Ala allows slow growth of the ∆argC strain in glucose.
evidence: This claim is based on prior experimental work by the authors' group.

claim: E383A ProA (ProA*) has severely reduced activity with γ-glutamyl semialdehyde (GSA), but substantially improved activity with N-acetylglutamyl semialdehyde (NAGSA).
source: Enzymatic assays show that E383A ProA (ProA*) has severely reduced activity with γ-glutamyl semialdehyde (GSA), but substantially improved activity with N-acetylglutamyl semialdehyde (NAGSA) (Khanal et al., 2015; McLoughlin and Copley, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Glu383 is in the active site of ProA.
source: Glu383 is in the active site of the enzyme; the change to Ala may create extra room to accommodate the larger substrate for ArgC, but at a cost to the ability to bind and orient the native substrate.
evidence: This claim is based on structural knowledge of the enzyme.

claim: The change of Glu383 to Ala may create extra room to accommodate the larger substrate for ArgC, but at a cost to the ability to bind and orient the native substrate.
source: Glu383 is in the active site of the enzyme; the change to Ala may create extra room to accommodate the larger substrate for ArgC, but at a cost to the ability to bind and orient the native substrate.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the structural consequences of the mutation.

claim: The poor efficiency of the weak-link ProA* creates strong selective pressure for improvement of both proline and arginine synthesis during growth of ∆argC E. coli on glucose as a sole carbon source.
source: The poor efficiency of the weak-link ProA* creates strong selective pressure for improvement of both proline and arginine synthesis during growth of ∆argC E. coli on glucose as a sole carbon source.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the metabolic constraints.

claim: Eight replicate populations of ∆argC proA* E. coli were evolved in minimal medium supplemented with glucose and proline for up to 1000 generations.
source: We evolved eight replicate populations of ∆argC proA* E. coli in minimal medium supplemented with glucose and proline for up to 1000 generations to identify mechanisms by which the impairment in arginine synthesis could be alleviated.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: The gene encoding the weak-link enzyme amplified in all eight populations.
source: The gene encoding the 'weak-link' enzyme amplified in all eight populations, but mutations improving the newly needed activity occurred in only one.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the evolution experiment.

claim: Mutations improving the newly needed activity occurred in only one population.
source: The gene encoding the 'weak-link' enzyme amplified in all eight populations, but mutations improving the newly needed activity occurred in only one.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the evolution experiment.

claim: Most adaptive mutations occurred elsewhere in the genome.
source: Most adaptive mutations occurred elsewhere in the genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-genome sequencing.

claim: Some mutations increase expression of the enzyme upstream of the weak-link enzyme, pushing material through the dysfunctional metabolic pathway.
source: Some mutations increase expression of the enzyme upstream of the weak-link enzyme, pushing material through the dysfunctional metabolic pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on ArgB expression and protein levels.

claim: Some mutations enhance production of a co-substrate for a downstream enzyme, thereby pulling material through the pathway.
source: Others enhance production of a co-substrate for a downstream enzyme, thereby pulling material through the pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on carbamoyl phosphate synthetase activity.

claim: Most of the mutations that enhance production of a co-substrate for a downstream enzyme are detrimental in wild-type E. coli.
source: Most of these latter mutations are detrimental in wild-type E. coli, and thus would require reversion or compensation once a sufficient new activity has evolved.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fitness competition assays.

claim: Growth rate of ∆argC proA* E. coli increased 3-fold within a few hundred generations of evolution in M9/glucose/proline.
source: Growth rate of ∆argC proA* E. coli increased 3-fold within a few hundred generations of evolution in M9/glucose/proline
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Over the course of the experiment, growth rate increased 2.5–3.5-fold for all eight populations.
source: Over the course of the experiment, growth rate increased 2.5–3.5-fold for all eight populations (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: proA* was present in at least six copies by generation 300 in all eight populations.
source: proA* was present in at least six copies by generation 300 in all eight populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Six of the populations maintained 6–9 copies of proA* for the remainder of the adaptation.
source: Six of the populations maintained 6–9 copies for the remainder of the adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: proA* copy number in population 2 increased to as many as 20 copies.
source: proA* copy number in population 2 increased to as many as 20 copies.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In population 3, proA* copy number dropped to three by generation 400.
source: In population 3, proA* copy number dropped to three by generation 400.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The amplified region in population 2 was unusually small, spanning only 4.9 kb and resulting in co-amplification of only two other genes besides proBA*.
source: The amplified region in population 2 was unusually small, spanning only 4.9 kb and resulting in co-amplification of only two other genes besides proBA*.
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Population 2 appeared to have a second region of amplification of 18.5 kb.
source: Population 2 also appeared to have a second region of amplification of 18.5 kb.
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The amplified regions in the other seven populations ranged from 41.1 to 163.8 kb, encompassing between 55 and 177 genes.
source: In contrast, the amplified regions in the other seven populations ranged from 41.1 to 163.8 kb, encompassing between 55 and 177 genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The variation in proA* copy number is attributed to differences in the size of the amplified region on the genome.
source: We attribute the variation in proA* copy number to these differences in the size of the amplified region on the genome.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed correlation between amplification size and copy number, supported by citations to prior work on fitness costs of amplification.

claim: The population with the smallest amplified region (4.9 kb, population 2) carries fewer multicopy genes and thus should incur a lower fitness cost, allowing proA* to reach a higher copy number.
source: The population with the smallest amplified region (4.9 kb, population 2) carries fewer multicopy genes and thus should incur a lower fitness cost, allowing proA* to reach a higher copy number (Adler et al., 2014; Kugelberg et al., 2006; Pettersson et al., 2009; Reams et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and is supported by citations to prior work on fitness costs of amplification.

claim: A mutation in proA* that changes Phe372 to Leu was observed in population 3.
source: In fact, a mutation in proA* that changes Phe372 to Leu (Figure 5A) was observed in population 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data and is illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Introduction of the F372L mutation into the parental strain increased growth rate by 75%.
source: Introduction of this mutation into the parental strain (which carried proA*) increased growth rate by 75% (Figure 5B), confirming that the mutation is adaptive.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No mutations in proA* were identified in any of the other populations.
source: Notably, no mutations in proA* were identified in any of the other populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data from all eight populations.

claim: The F372L mutation is not beneficial on its own.
source: Strains with either wild-type or F372L ProA did not grow after eight days. Thus, the F372L mutation is not beneficial on its own, and the combined effect of the two mutations is greater than the sum of their individual effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The combined effect of the E383A and F372L mutations is greater than the sum of their individual effects.
source: Thus, the F372L mutation is not beneficial on its own, and the combined effect of the two mutations is greater than the sum of their individual effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The kcat/KM,NAGSA for ProA** is 3.6-fold higher than that of ProA*.
source: The kcat/KM,NAGSA for ProA** is 3.6-fold higher than that of ProA* and nearly 80-fold higher than that for ProA.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic assay data shown in Table 2.

claim: The kcat/KM,NAGSA for ProA** is nearly 80-fold higher than that for wild-type ProA.
source: The kcat/KM,NAGSA for ProA** is 3.6-fold higher than that of ProA* and nearly 80-fold higher than that for ProA.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic assay data shown in Table 2.

claim: There is no difference between kcat/KM,GSA for ProA* and ProA**.
source: In contrast, there is no difference between kcat/KM,GSA for ProA* and ProA**.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic assay data shown in Table 2.

claim: proA** was present in 9% of the sequencing reads by generation 270.
source: proA** was present in 9% of the sequencing reads by generation 270.
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: By generation 440, the frequency of proA** had risen to 21% of sequencing reads.
source: By the time deamplification of proA* had occurred at generation 440, the frequency of proA** had risen to 21% of sequencing reads.
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: By the end of the adaptation, proA** was fixed in the population.
source: By the end of the adaptation, proA** was fixed in the population, yet three copies remained in the genome, suggesting that ProA** does not have sufficient neo-ArgC activity to be present at a single copy in the genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Three copies of proA** remained in the genome at the end of the adaptation, suggesting that ProA** does not have sufficient neo-ArgC activity to be present at a single copy in the genome.
source: By the end of the adaptation, proA** was fixed in the population, yet three copies remained in the genome, suggesting that ProA** does not have sufficient neo-ArgC activity to be present at a single copy in the genome.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed copy number data.

claim: The first mutation to appear in all populations was either an 82 bp deletion in the rph pseudogene directly upstream of pyrE or a C→T mutation in the intergenic region between rph and pyrE.
source: The first mutation to appear in all populations was either an 82 bp deletion in the rph pseudogene directly upstream of pyrE or a C→T mutation in the intergenic region between rph and pyrE.
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data.

claim: The rph-pyrE mutations occurred by 100 generations and prior to amplification of proBA*.
source: These mutations occurred by 100 generations and prior to amplification of proBA*.
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data.

claim: Both of the rph-pyrE mutations have arisen in other E. coli evolution experiments, and have been shown to restore a known PyrE deficiency in the BW25113 E. coli strain.
source: Both of these mutations have arisen in other E. coli evolution experiments, and have been shown to restore a known PyrE deficiency in the BW25113 E. coli strain (Blank et al., 2014; Bonekamp et al., 1984; Conrad et al., 2009; Jensen, 1993; Knöppel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The 82 bp deletion in rph increases growth rate of the parental AM187 strain by 55%.
source: The 82 bp deletion in rph increases growth rate of the parental AM187 strain by 55% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements.

claim: The rph-pyrE mutations are general adaptations to growth in minimal medium and do not pertain to the selective pressures caused by the weak-link enzyme ProA*.
source: Thus, these mutations are general adaptations to growth in minimal medium and do not pertain to the selective pressures caused by the weak-link enzyme ProA*.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and prior knowledge about these mutations.

claim: A mutation in ygcB occurred early in four populations.
source: A mutation in ygcB occurred early in four populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data.

claim: The ygcB mutation changes Ala390 to Val in Cas3, a nuclease/helicase in the Type I CRISPR/Cas system in E. coli.
source: This mutation changes Ala390 to Val in Cas3, a nuclease/helicase in the Type I CRISPR/Cas system in E. coli (Howard et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome sequencing data and citation to prior research on Cas3.

claim: The ygcB mutation showed no significant change in growth rate when introduced into the parental strain.
source: We introduced this mutation into the genome of the parent AM187 and compared the growth rates of the mutant and AM187 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Surprisingly, we saw no significant change in growth rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements.

claim: The ygcB mutation is most likely a neutral hitchhiker.
source: Thus, the ygcB mutation is most likely a neutral hitchhiker.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the lack of fitness effect.

claim: All eight final populations contained mutations in the intergenic region upstream of argB and downstream of kanr.
source: All eight final populations contained mutations in the intergenic region upstream of argB and downstream of kanr.
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The argB upstream mutations were fixed in two populations, and present at frequencies of 9–82% in the other populations.
source: These mutations were fixed in two populations, and present at frequencies of 9–82% in the other populations (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Six of the argB mutations increased growth rate by 36–61% when introduced into the parental strain AM187.
source: The mutations increased growth rate by 36–61% (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The argB upstream mutations increased the abundance of ArgB protein by 2.6–8.2-fold.
source: However, levels of ArgB protein increased 2.6–8.2-fold (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Levels of mRNAs for argB and argH were little affected by the argB upstream mutations.
source: Levels of mRNAs for argB and argH, which is immediately downstream of argB, were little affected by the mutations (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The argB upstream mutations increase translational efficiency of argB mRNA.
source: These data suggest that the mutations upstream of argB increase translational efficiency of argB mRNA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that protein levels increased without corresponding mRNA increases.

claim: An increase in the amount of ArgB will increase production of NAGP, the substrate for the weak-link enzyme ProA*.
source: An increase in the amount of ArgB will increase production of NAGP, the substrate for the weak-link enzyme ProA* (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the metabolic pathway shown in Figure 2.

claim: The level of ArgH is 64% higher in AM187 compared to AM407.
source: The level of ArgH is 64% higher in AM187, probably due to increased transcription of the operon.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The level of ArgB is 2.3-fold lower in AM187 compared to AM407.
source: In contrast, the level of ArgB is 2.3-fold lower, suggesting that the altered structure upstream of argB mRNA diminishes translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The growth rates of AM187 and AM407 are identical.
source: Despite these changes, the growth rates of AM187 and AM407 are identical (µ = 0.27 ± 0.01 h−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements.

claim: Growth rate of AM187 improves substantially when ArgB levels are increased by 25-fold from a low-copy plasmid.
source: Growth rate of AM187 improves substantially when ArgB levels are increased by 25-fold, demonstrating that the beneficial effect of the mutations we observed in the evolved strains is not simply due to compensation for the 2.3-fold decrease in ArgB caused by replacement of argC with kanr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Eight different mutations in carB were found in six of the evolved populations: four missense mutations, three deletions (≥12 bp), and one 21 bp duplication.
source: We found eight different mutations in carB in six of the evolved populations: four missense mutations, three deletions (≥12 bp), and one 21 bp duplication (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CarB forms a complex with CarA to catalyze production of carbamoyl phosphate from glutamine, bicarbonate, and two molecules of ATP.
source: CarB, the large subunit of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase (CPS), forms a complex with CarA to catalyze production of carbamoyl phosphate from glutamine, bicarbonate, and two molecules of ATP (Equation 1).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about carbamoyl phosphate synthetase.

claim: Seven of the eight mutations found in carB affect residues in the allosteric domain of CarB.
source: Seven of the eight mutations found in carB affect residues in the allosteric domain of CarB.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: All carB mutations decreased kcat/Km,ATP by 34–63%, with the exception of the mutation that changes Lys966 to Glu, which nearly doubles kcat/Km,ATP.
source: All mutations decreased kcat/Km,ATP by 34–63%, with the exception of the mutation that changes Lys966 to Glu, which nearly doubles kcat/Km,ATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic assay data shown in Table 3.

claim: None of the carB mutations affected the enzyme's ability to couple ATP hydrolysis with carbamoyl phosphate production.
source: None of the mutations affected the enzyme's ability to couple ATP hydrolysis with carbamoyl phosphate production (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Five of the carB variants showed complete loss of allosteric regulation.
source: Five of the variants showed complete loss of allosteric regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic assay data shown in Table 3 and Figure 7D-E.

claim: Three of the carB mutations (K966E, ∆12 bp at nt 2906, and ∆132 bp at nt 2986) increased growth rate of AM187.
source: Three of the mutations (K966E, ∆12 bp at nt 2906, and ∆132 bp at nt 2986) increased growth rate (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The two carB mutations that caused loss of UMP inhibition (∆12 bp at nt 2906 and ∆132 bp at nt 2986) showed the greatest increase in growth rate (47–54%).
source: The two mutations that caused loss of UMP inhibition (∆12 bp at nt 2906 and ∆132 bp at nt 2986) showed the greatest increase in growth rate (47–54%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The K966E carB mutation increased growth rate of AM187 by 26%.
source: The mutation that increased CPS catalytic activity (K966E) increased growth rate by 26%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The G369V carB mutation does not improve growth rate of AM187.
source: The G369V mutation does not improve growth rate of AM187, which is not surprising because its major effect is to increase ornithine activation at high ornithine concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Adding uracil to the medium increased the growth rate of AM187, but did not affect the growth rate of AM327.
source: Adding uracil to the medium increased the growth rate of AM187, but did not affect the growth rate of AM327, suggesting that pyrimidine synthesis is no longer insufficient after acquisition of the ∆82 bp rph-pyrE mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Adding arginine restored growth of both AM187 and AM327 to wild-type levels.
source: In contrast, adding arginine restored growth of both strains to wild-type levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The two carB deletion mutations that abolished allosteric regulation (Δ12 bp at nt 2906 and Δ132 bp at nt 2986) significantly decreased growth rate in wild-type E. coli.
source: The two deletion mutations that abolished allosteric regulation (Δ12 bp at nt 2906 and Δ132 bp at nt 2986) significantly decreased growth rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The K966E carB mutation slightly decreases growth rate in wild-type E. coli.
source: The K966E mutation, which increases kcat/KM,ATP by 64% but shifts the balance between the regulatory effects of UMP and ornithine by modestly increasing UMP inhibition and decreasing ornithine activation, also slightly decreases growth rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The G369V carB mutation actually increased growth rate in wild-type E. coli.
source: The G369V mutation, which diminishes inhibition by UMP but substantially increases activation by ornithine, actually increased growth rate, suggesting that the balance between the regulatory effects of UMP and ornithine in the wild-type CarB may not be optimal after the rph-pyrE mutation improves pyrimidine synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Many of the carB mutations provide a fitness improvement when arginine synthesis is compromised, but will be detrimental once an efficient neo-ArgC has emerged.
source: These results suggest that many of the carB mutations provide a fitness improvement when arginine synthesis is compromised, but will be detrimental once an efficient neo-ArgC has emerged.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the fitness data in different genetic backgrounds.

claim: Homologous recombination after an initial duplication event occurs in ~1 of every 100 cell divisions.
source: Homologous recombination after an initial duplication event is orders of magnitude more frequent, occurring in ~1 of every 100 cell divisions (Reams et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Point mutations occur at a frequency between 10−9 and 10−10 per nucleotide per cell division depending on the genomic location.
source: Point mutations occur at a frequency between 10−9 and 10−10 per nucleotide per cell division depending on the genomic location (Jee et al., 2016), and thus between 10−6 and 10−7 per gene per cell division for a gene the size of proA.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Homologous recombination between replicating chromosomes in a cell could result in a selective allelic sweep long before a second beneficial mutation occurs in a different allele in the amplified array.
source: Thus, homologous recombination between replicating chromosomes in a cell could result in a selective allelic sweep (Figure 9) long before a second beneficial mutation occurs in a different allele in the amplified array.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the relative frequencies of mutation and recombination.

claim: Heterozygosity among proA* alleles was lost within 500 generations.
source: This is indeed the result that we observed; heterozygosity among proA* alleles was lost within 500 generations (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by population genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mutations that improve the neo-ArgC activity of ProA* are uncommon or their fitness effects are smaller than those caused by mutations elsewhere in the genome that also improve arginine synthesis.
source: While growth rate improved substantially in all populations, a beneficial mutation in proA* arose in only one, suggesting either that mutations that improve the neo-ArgC activity are uncommon, or that their fitness effects are smaller than those caused by mutations elsewhere in the genome that also improve arginine synthesis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that only one population evolved a proA* mutation despite strong selective pressure.

claim: The process of evolution of a new enzyme by gene duplication and divergence is inextricably intertwined with mutations elsewhere in the genome that improve fitness by different mechanisms.
source: Our results demonstrate that mutations elsewhere in the genome play an important role during the process of gene amplification and divergence when the inefficient activity of a weak-link enzyme limits fitness. Thus, the process of evolution of a new enzyme by gene duplication and divergence is inextricably intertwined with mutations elsewhere in the genome that improve fitness by different mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the overall results of the study.

claim: The prevalence of adaptive mutations outside of proA* is likely a result of both a limited number of adaptive routes for improving the neo-ArgC activity of ProA* and a larger target size for other beneficial mutations.
source: The prevalence of adaptive mutations outside of proA* is likely a result of both a limited number of adaptive routes for improving the neo-ArgC activity of ProA* and a larger target size for other beneficial mutations (Ilhan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Directed evolution experiments often show a limited number of paths for improvement of enzymatic activity.
source: Directed evolution experiments often show a limited number of paths for improvement of enzymatic activity (Aharoni et al., 2005; Sunden et al., 2015; Weinreich et al., 2006), which reflects the stringent requirements for optimal placement of substrate-binding and catalytic residues in active sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are multiple ways in which allosteric inhibition of CarB by UMP can be lost.
source: In contrast, there are multiple ways in which allosteric inhibition of CarB by UMP can be lost, and multiple ways in which translation efficiency of argB mRNA can be improved.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation of multiple different mutations with similar effects.

claim: There are multiple ways in which translation efficiency of argB mRNA can be improved.
source: In contrast, there are multiple ways in which allosteric inhibition of CarB by UMP can be lost, and multiple ways in which translation efficiency of argB mRNA can be improved.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation of multiple different mutations with similar effects.
